input:
Principle

At the heart of every heat exchanger lies a deceptively simple idea: heat is transferred from a hot stream to a cold stream through a separating wall, and the two streams themselves never actually mix with one another. The duty of the exchanger, denoted $Q$, is the rate at which heat crosses that wall, and it can be obtained from an energy balance written on either stream: for each stream, the duty is equal to the mass flow multiplied by the heat capacity and by the change in temperature experienced by that stream, and, provided no heat is lost to the surroundings, the balance on the hot stream and the balance on the cold stream will give exactly the same duty.

Temperature does not remain constant along the exchanger. The hot stream cools as it gives up its heat and the cold stream warms as it receives heat, and consequently the temperature difference between the streams, which is the driving force for the heat transfer, varies from point to point along the length. The overall heat transfer coefficient, denoted $U$, is a quantity that conveniently gathers all of the resistances in the path into a single figure: convection in the hot stream, conduction through the wall, and convection in the cold stream, all referred to a stated area basis. The sizing relation then states that the duty is the product of the overall coefficient, the heat transfer area, denoted $A$, and a mean temperature difference, and where the coefficient is constant along the exchanger, the mean that makes this relation exact is the log-mean temperature difference, denoted $\Delta T_{lm}$, which is formed from the temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger.

The flow arrangement plays a major role in how the driving force behaves. In counter-current flow the streams enter at opposite ends, the temperature difference remains comparatively even along the length, and the cold stream can actually leave hotter than the hot stream leaves. In co-current flow, by contrast, the streams enter at the same end, the difference is at its largest at the inlet and falls along the length, and no such crossing of the outlet temperatures is possible. At each end of the exchanger, the difference between the hot and cold temperatures is referred to as a terminal difference, and the smaller terminal difference is the tight end of the unit.

Equipment

The shell-and-tube exchanger is the standard industrial form, and it is the form against which the alternatives are usually measured. In this configuration, one stream flows inside a bundle of tubes while the other stream flows across the bundle inside a surrounding shell. Baffles are provided to support the tubes and to direct the shell-side stream repeatedly across the bundle, Tube sheets fix the ends of the tubes, and channels at each end distribute the tube-side stream among the tubes. The differential thermal expansion that arises between the shell and the tubes is accommodated by means of a floating head or an expansion joint, depending on the severity of the temperature difference between the streams.

Other forms exist to serve other duties. A plate exchanger clamps corrugated plates with gaskets between them: the resulting unit is compact, it can readily be opened for cleaning, and the gaskets inevitably bound the pressure and temperature that it can serve. An air-cooled exchanger passes the hot stream through finned tubes while fans move air across the fins, and it is typically chosen where cooling water is scarce where water is too warm for the duty. The selection among the forms turns on pressure, temperature, fouling tendency, access for cleaning, and the corrosiveness of the streams, with the stream that attacks the metal being placed on the side that can be built in the resistant material or cleaned most readily.

Worked example

The task is to size an exchanger for a stated duty, using only the quantities that have been given in the principle part. The duty is taken from the balance on the hot stream: the mass flow of the hot stream, its heat capacity, and its temperature change are the given quantities, and their product is the duty. The terminal differences are then obtained from the terminal temperatures: the hot stream enters at its inlet temperature and leaves at its outlet temperature, the cold stream enters cold and leaves warm, and the difference between the hot and cold temperatures at each end of the exchanger gives the terminal difference at that end. From the two terminal differences, the log-mean temperature difference is calculated. The overall coefficient is taken as the value given for the service in the principle part. Finally, the area is obtained by dividing the duty by the product of the overall coefficient and the log-mean temperature difference.

The example closes with two checks on the same data. Repeating the terminal-difference step for the other flow arrangement, with no change in any terminal temperature, shows the counter-current arrangement holding the larger mean difference and therefore needing the smaller area. Overall, the example demonstrates that a sizing of this kind rests on the duty, the coefficient, and the mean temperature difference, with the flow arrangement entering through the terminal differences alone.

Limits

The simple model set out in the principle part holds where the overall coefficient is steady along the exchanger and the streams remain in a single phase. Where a stream boils or condenses, however, the mechanism of heat transfer changes along the length, the coefficient varies with position, and a single mean temperature difference no longer adequately describes the local rates; in such cases the exchanger is rated in sections, each with its own coefficient and its own temperature difference.

Service introduces further limits that the clean calculation does not take into account. Deposits foul the surfaces and add resistance, so a coefficient that has been measured or computed for clean surfaces will overstate the duty after a period of time on stream; design practice allows for fouling by adding a fouling resistance to the clean resistances. Alongside these thermal considerations stand mechanical limits: pressure containment, differential expansion, and flow-induced vibration all bound the design independently of the sizing relation.

In summary, the chapter has set out the sizing of a heat exchanger from an energy balance, a mean temperature difference, and an overall coefficient; the equipment forms in which that sizing is realised; and the conditions under which the simple model stops describing the unit.
